Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data, but their extensive computational requirements can limit their deployment. To make these models more practical, we propose a new technique called Pruning In Time (PIT) that optimizes TCNs for temporal data by combining two efficient methods: temporal pruning and the Chunky Tensor Core (CTC) architecture. By leveraging both techniques, PIT achieves superior performance compared to other optimization methods, including sparsity-aware training and pruning-in-time alone. Our experiments demonstrate that PIT can significantly enhance the performance of TCNs on both classification and regression tasks, reducing computational latency by up to 5x without compromising accuracy. Furthermore, PIT's efficiency is showcased through a real-world application involving the prediction of cardiac arrest risk. To address this limitation, a new method called PDM has been developed by modifying the RDM method to use linear regression and a more comprehensive model of reactivity, resulting in improved accuracy and faster computation times. However, the optimized variant of PDM, which is the most accurate, is too complex to model large molecules, while the two less optimized variants are more practical but less accurate. To make the most accurate variant more manageable for large molecules, a new algorithm has been developed by combining linear regression with a simplified version of the optimized variant, and this combined algorithm has been shown to produce high-quality results for large molecules. Furthermore, the ability of the RDM and PDM methods to model chemical reactions has been demonstrated, and the code for these methods is publicly available. Due to its high accuracy, the PDM method is particularly useful for modeling molecules and reactions in the context of COVID-19 research. In addition, the ability of the RDM and PDM methods to model chemical compounds and reactions has been validated using multiple metrics, including the Tanimoto similarity coefficient, the RMSD metric, and the accuracy of predicted atoms and bonds. The PDM method has also been compared to other machine learning methods for modeling molecules and reactions, and it has been found to be the most accurate for modeling large molecules and reactions involving multiple atoms. The proposed DDAUnet model builds upon the standard Unet architecture by incorporating advanced features such as dense blocks, reverse block, and dense attention modules to effectively utilize input data and extract valuable information. The dense block and reverse block features are combined using a dense fusion block to reduce information redundancy. The attention weight is derived from the dense block and reverse block features. Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a key to various applications such as text mining and information extraction. Unlike other NLP tasks that focus solely on sentence-level analysis, NER involves identifying and categorizing entities within a sentence. A significant challenge in NER arises from the nested nature of certain entities, where a single entity can be fully or partially contained within another entity of the same or different type. To address this issue, existing methods often employ sequential models or employ techniques such as BERT, yet these approaches overlook the holistic structure of nested entities. In contrast, our proposed framework views NER as a holistic parsing task, where entities are analyzed as a whole rather than as individual parts. Furthermore, we introduce a novel model that incorporates a bidirectional encoder and a decoder to capture both local and global dependencies within sentences. The decoder consists of multiple decoding units, each capable of handling entities of varying lengths and types. We also introduce a novel decoding unit for nested entities and demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments on the standard CoNLL-2003 NER dataset. The results show that our proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art models such as BERT and Bi-LSTM on the Chinese and Korean datasets, respectively. Multilingual individuals, who are fluent in two or more languages, interact with others in various settings, including online platforms and everyday conversations, by switching between languages or blending them. Code-switching and code-mixing occur when this happens, involving the use of two or more languages within the same text, utterance, or conversation. This phenomenon is prevalent in many multilingual communities and has significant implications for the development of NLP systems. However, the field of NLP has largely overlooked code-mixing until recently, with few studies exploring its intricacies. This paper aims to address this knowledge gap by discussing the challenges and considerations of NLP in multilingual societies, with a focus on code-mixing. It delves into the complexities of data collection, annotation, and processing, as well as the difficulties in training and evaluating models. Furthermore, it highlights the need for more robust and adaptable NLP systems that can effectively handle code-mixing in real-world applications. This paper also presents an initial attempt to create a comprehensive taxonomy of code-mixing NLP tasks, which can serve as a starting point for further research and collaboration within the field. This taxonomy is available online at https://github.com/CodeMixNLP-Society/CodeMixNLP-Taxonomy. The spread of misinformation through social media platforms has been exacerbated by the growing divide between physical communities, or the Big Sort. This phenomenon has led to increased isolation within homogeneous areas, where residents share similar viewpoints and news sources. As a result, false information can spread rapidly within these localized echo chambers. This study examines the connection between the Big Sort and the dissemination of misinformation by analyzing Reddit user activity across 600 U.S. counties. Our findings reveal that misinformation dissemination is more prevalent in counties with greater population homogeneity, as measured by the Index of Diversity, and this association holds true even after controlling for factors like population size, urban vs. rural settings, and economic conditions. Furthermore, we discovered that the relationship between diversity and misinformation dissemination is particularly pronounced in counties with higher levels of civic engagement and news consumption. Our research suggests that targeting false information at the local level, through community-driven initiatives, may be an effective approach, especially in areas with a high level of civic engagement. However, this strategy may be less effective in areas with low population diversity and limited civic engagement. To further explore this idea, we propose a framework for evaluating the efficacy of local interventions in reducing misinformation dissemination. Previous studies have demonstrated that Translation Memory (TM) can enhance Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance, especially in domains with limited training data. However, existing approaches rely on bilingual corpora and suffer from high costs in both time and money. In contrast, we propose utilizing monolingual corpora as a low-cost alternative, which we term Monolingual Translation Memory (MTM). To effectively integrate MTM with NMT, we present two models: a direct extension to the source language encoder and a retrieval-based model inspired by neural TM. Experimental results indicate that our simple yet effective approach can achieve significant improvements over baseline NMT models on low-resource languages and domains with limited parallel data. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can adapt to new domains with minimal data, achieving a 19.4% boost in BLEU score on the low-resource domain adaptation task. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/zhengyangwang/Neural-NMT-with-MTM.

Cross-domain recommendation has become a prominent technique in addressing the issue of limited data in individual domains. Although various methods have been developed to tackle this challenge, there remains a significant gap in research for domains with diverse and complex sparsity patterns. In this study, we introduce a novel framework for multi-sparse-domain collaborative recommendation that takes into account the unique characteristics of each domain. Specifically, we propose an Enhanced Comprehensively Aspect Preference Learning (ECAPL) model to capture users' diverse and intricate preferences within each domain. The ECAPL model incorporates an attention-based neural network and a multi-task learning framework to effectively integrate cross-domain information. Furthermore, we introduce a Domain-Specific Preference Learning (DSPL) module to address the issue of data scarcity in each domain. The DSPL module utilizes a combination of contrastive learning and self-supervised learning to enhance the robustness of user-domain representations. Through extensive experiments on the Amazon Product Review dataset, our proposed framework consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple domains, including both dense and sparse domains. The code for this study is publicly available on GitHub. Additionally, we provide a pre-trained model for the Amazon Product Review dataset on GitHub. This pre-trained model demonstrates superior performance compared to existing methods on multiple evaluation metrics. However, we cannot guarantee the optimal performance of this pre-trained model for other datasets or scenarios. Furthermore, we highlight the challenges and potential research directions for cross-domain recommendation in the presence of diverse and complex sparsity patterns. This includes the difficulty of selecting suitable base models and the absence of universally applicable evaluation metrics. The study of epidemic models on dynamic networks can provide valuable insights into the spread of diseases and other infectious phenomena. This research focuses on a specific SIR model where individuals reconnect to the network in response to an epidemic, and we investigate how the model's behavior changes when the connection strategy is random and unaffected by the epidemic. We discovered that introducing a random rewiring mechanism can significantly slow the spread of diseases, even in highly connected networks prone to rapid epidemic outbreaks. Notably, this phenomenon occurs regardless of the degree distribution of the network. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the model's behavior is characterized by a critical threshold, below which the epidemic spreads quickly, and above which it spreads slowly. This threshold is defined by the product of the average rewiring rate and the probability of infection. Our research also highlights the importance of dynamic network analysis in understanding the spread of diseases and other infectious phenomena. Additionally, we propose a simplified static network model that captures the model's behavior near the critical threshold, and this static model can be applied to analyze various dynamic network scenarios. This research provides valuable insights into the prevention and control of disease outbreaks in dynamic networks. where a limited pool of labeled images is selected for annotation based on predicted 
uncertainty. In our study, we develop an active learning framework for large-scale 
uncertainty selection, starting with a pre-trained model and a modestly sized labeled 
dataset. We test this framework on the ImageNet dataset with over 14 million possible 
training images, using a relatively small pool of 100,000 labeled images. Our results

labels, and a 12% better top-1 accuracy with twice as many labels. Our active 
learning approach also enables efficient selection of high-quality labels for transfer 
learning tasks, with a 5% improvement in top-1 accuracy on the CIFAR-100 dataset.

Temporal action detection is a challenging task that involves pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. Unlike classification tasks that only require identifying the presence or absence of an action, detection tasks demand precise timing information. A major difficulty in this task arises from the vast range of possible action durations, making it essential to design models that can effectively handle both short and long action periods. In this study, we present a Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) that addresses this issue by incorporating two separate context aggregation pathways. The first pathway focuses on aggregating short-action information within a limited temporal window, while the second pathway targets longer-action periods by exploring the entire video timeline. To train the DCAN model, we employ a dual strategy, utilizing a combination of classification and bounding box regression techniques. The proposed DCAN model is extensively evaluated on the ActivityNet dataset, yielding superior performance compared to state-of-the-art models. Notably, our model achieves exceptional results on previously unexplored long-action categories, demonstrating its capacity to handle both brief and extended action periods. Continual learning with pre-trained models has achieved remarkable results in various tasks, including image classification and natural language processing. However, these models are typically trained on a single task and require significant fine-tuning for each new task, which contradicts the fundamental principle of continual learning. In this paper, we challenge the notion that pre-trained models are inherently suitable for continual learning by comparing their performance to a simple baseline that combines data from multiple tasks without any fine-tuning. Our results show that this baseline, which simply averages the features of pre-trained models for each task, outperforms the usual practice of continual learning. This counterintuitive finding suggests that continual learning with pre-trained models is actually a form of overfitting, where each model is excessively tailored to its individual task. We also explore several extensions to this baseline, including adding a shared neural network, using a single model for all tasks, and incorporating memory mechanisms, which can further improve performance. Our research indicates that pre-trained models can be successfully used for continual learning, but only when they are used in a more sophisticated way than the usual practice of continual learning. We examined the performance of various validation techniques, including k-fold cross-validation, which is commonly employed despite the limited number of samples in NLP datasets. Our analysis revealed that k-fold CV can lead to reduced variance when selecting model parameters, which is particularly beneficial when combining multiple runs. We observed that k-fold CV often outperformed traditional methods such as single-split training and validation, stratified k-fold CV, and random search. Notably, even with relatively small datasets like CoNLL-2003, k-fold CV achieved comparable results to those obtained with larger datasets like CoQA and SQuAD v1.1. Our findings suggest that NLP practitioners should consider using k-fold CV when tuning model parameters, especially when combining multiple runs. We also found that the optimal k value depends on the specific task and dataset, but generally falls within the range of 5 to 10. We propose that the k-fold CV method should be widely adopted as the default validation technique for tuning model parameters in NLP. We introduce a new compact function representation, called the 'Path Table', which expresses the Minimum Energy (ME) and Most Probable Explanation (MPE) functions in a more efficient manner. This novel approach enables us to precisely determine the exact values of ME and MPE functions at any given node, even if the node is part of a cyclic path. By utilizing the Path Table, we can accurately compute the ME and MPE values for any single node in a polynomial time, whereas previous methods require exponential time for certain cyclic graphs. Furthermore, we can derive the optimal values for a specific node function that satisfies certain constraints across all possible assignments, which can be achieved in O(n^3.5) time, a significant improvement over the previous O(2^n) time. This new representation is particularly beneficial for large-scale graphical models with a small number of interacting variables. We demonstrate the efficacy of the Path Table by applying it to the task of neural machine translation, which involves complex cyclic dependencies. Our results show that the Path Table can achieve a high accuracy of 43.1 BLEU score, a significant improvement over the previous state-of-the-art of 41.9 BLEU score. This improvement is achieved with a much more compact model that has 1/10th the parameters of the previous best model. This new representation can be used in any graphical model that involves cyclic dependencies, and we anticipate that it will be widely adopted in the field of computer science. A precise method of measuring absorption coefficients in gases is single-beam absorption spectroscopy. Typically, this method relies on cross-correlation analysis between the light transmitted through the gas and a reference light, which is not affected by the gas. In this study, we utilize ultracold strontium atoms in a state of hyperfine polarization to achieve absorption measurements with high accuracy. By using a narrow laser to excite a specific transition within the atomic ensemble, we are able to minimize the uncertainty associated with the position of the absorption feature. Our findings demonstrate that even without this localization, the photon recoil effect can still limit the precision of the measurement. As a result, we find that a larger number of atoms is necessary to achieve the same level of accuracy. This discovery has implications for the application of this method to study other types of atoms or molecules that are more difficult to polarize. In such cases, the photon recoil effect may become the dominant limitation, and therefore, it is essential to consider it when designing experiments. In the case of the strontium atoms used in this study, the required number of atoms is on the order of $10^{10}$. This level of precision can be achieved using a relatively simple setup, which is an important consideration for future experiments. By examining the energy spectra and power density spectra, we found a low-frequency Quasi-Periodic Oscillation with a frequency of approximately 0.044 Hz and a fractional amplitude of 0.04 during the peak outburst phase. Additionally, we detected a cyclotron line with an energy of 13.2 keV, confirming previous findings from RXTE. Our analysis revealed that the line was present throughout the outburst, with a constant energy but varying equivalent width. Notably, the 0.1-20 Hz power density spectrum exhibited a power spectrum with multiple components, including a flat top and a broad hump, with the latter's amplitude decreasing as the outburst peaked. Our results suggest that the accretion disk's inner radius expanded during the outburst's peak phase, with a radius of approximately 10 km. However, we found no correlation between the inner radius and the cyclotron line energy, nor did we observe any significant changes in the disk's inner radius during the outburst. Our findings provide valuable insights into the behavior of IGR J19294+1816 and its accretion disk during the 2019 outburst. A novel technique called source separation coding is proposed, offering a flexible and efficient approach to image and video processing. Unlike conventional methods, source separation coding separates the coding process into two distinct steps: encoding raw data samples and reconstructing the original image or video from these encoded values. This technique's effectiveness is demonstrated through its application to two complex problems: color image demosaicing and compressed video recovery. By optimizing the codes used in these instances, significant improvements are achieved, outperforming existing methods and serving as a valuable insight into the development of novel compression techniques. Code optimization strategies are also explored, including various methods for solving the nonconvex optimization problem posed by source separation coding. This research offers a new perspective on image and video compression and compression artifacts, providing a useful framework for the development of future compression techniques. We investigate in detail how topological entropy and factor complexity in subshifts behave under two types of variations: both natural and less natural changes in generating rules, specifically those defined by monoid morphisms and free group basis changes. Our findings reveal that while topological entropy exhibits consistent behavior under both types of variations, factor complexity can exhibit unpredictable behavior, particularly when free group basis changes are involved. Notably, we demonstrate that there exist free group basis changes which result in factor complexities that not only fail to compare to each other but also fail to compare to their initial values. This discovery provides a clear answer to a previously open question regarding the behavior of factor complexities in shift spaces. Furthermore, our research also provides a clear answer to a recently posed question by Stifel regarding the behavior of topological entropy in free group basis changes. Both of these findings are supported by concrete examples and counterexamples. Additionally, we outline a general framework for defining and analyzing the behavior of various properties, such as topological entropy and factor complexity, under both monoid morphisms and free group basis changes. This framework is demonstrated to be robust and can be applied across multiple contexts. Finally, we outline an open problem related to free group basis changes and suggest that further research is needed to fully understand the behavior of topological entropy and factor complexity in this context. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to new tasks without additional training or guidance is a key aspect of human intelligence that we refer to as cross-task generalization. In this research, we frame cross-task generalization as a retrieval problem where previously learned representations serve as a source of high-quality retrievals. We propose a novel, unsupervised method called Retrieval-Augmented Unsupervised Generalization (RAUG) that utilizes a memory bank of past experiences to guide self-supervised learning through an efficient and differentiable memory retrieval process. RAUG significantly outperforms baseline methods on multiple datasets and tasks, including the MNIST, SVHN, and CelebA datasets, and the tasks of single-image super-resolution, image-to-image translation, and colorization. Furthermore, our method exhibits impressive cross-task generalization performance, surpassing the current state-of-the-art methods on the unconditional image-to-image translation task by a substantial margin of 4.1% in the FID score when tested on the CelebA dataset without any training. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/zhengyangwang/RAUG.

Optimizing hyperparameters in a private setting is a significant challenge due to the limited availability of labeled data under privacy constraints and the difficulty of balancing model performance and data protection. This issue is particularly pronounced in the context of private deep learning, where achieving both high accuracy and robust privacy protection proves elusive. To address this problem, we propose a novel approach called Hyperparameter Optimization for Private Deep Learning (HOPL), which leverages a limited amount of public data to optimize hyperparameters in a private manner. This approach is efficient, as it reduces hyperparameter tuning time by an order of magnitude compared to traditional methods. Moreover, HOPL achieves superior private accuracy on multiple benchmark datasets, including the MNIST, CIFAR-10, and EMNIST datasets, with a $4\delta$ differential privacy guarantee. Notably, HOPL's performance surpasses state-of-the-art private models, such as Private End-to-End (PEPE), with a significant margin of up to 10% improvement in private accuracy. The source code of HOPL is publicly available on the GitHub repository https://github.com/yourgithublink/HOPL. HOPL's hyperparameter tuning framework can be adapted to other private machine learning models, and we provide a theoretical analysis of HOPL's privacy risk in the appendix. A significant challenge in processing images in the presence of rain is the distortion caused by rain, which complicates tasks such as image segmentation, object detection, and scene dehazing. Current methods to address this issue involve pre-processing the image to simulate a rain-free environment, which is not always feasible. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel approach to simultaneously generate a rain image from a rain-free image and remove the rain from an image with rain. This is achieved through a single neural network that performs two tasks: a rain-free image generation task and a rain removal task. By leveraging the AdvGAN loss function, we can train this network to accurately remove rain from images, even in scenarios with heavy rain. The proposed method is efficient and outperforms existing techniques, including a state-of-the-art method that requires a separate network for rain generation. Notably, our approach can be trained on a single dataset containing images with rain, without the need for a rain-free dataset. This is made possible by incorporating a rain generation adversarial loss function, which enables the network to learn the characteristics of rain and generate a rain image from a rain-free image. This allows the network to learn a rain image representation and remove actual rain from images. The proposed method is evaluated on a range of datasets, including synthetic and real-world images with rain, and achieves state-of-the-art performance. The code is publicly available on GitHub. By providing a flexible and efficient framework for rain removal, this approach has potential applications in various computer vision tasks. We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed acyclic graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we have developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Notably, combined with a prior observation, these results lead to fixed-parameter tractability for graphs with a limited number of directed cycles. Additionally, we have observed that the problem of finding an equivalent upward planar layout with the fewest number of new layers can be solved in parameterized time, given a graph parameter of size n, and we have introduced a simpler proof for the existence of an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth. Furthermore, we have introduced two new parameters, upward-width and up-branch-width, which are shown to be equivalent in their ability to distinguish directed acyclic graphs that are upward planar from those that are not. However, unlike treedepth and treewidth, these new parameters are NP-complete to determine at least one of them given an instance of a directed acyclic graph. Lastly, we have observed that the problem of determining whether a directed acyclic graph can be represented in an upward planar layout with a specific number of layers is fixed-parameter tractable based on the up-branch-width parameter. This research extends and refines prior findings on directed acyclic graphs and planar layouts. In contrast, the EKMP framework directly addresses constraints and obstacles as nonlinear hard constraints through the use of Lagrange multipliers. The resulting penalty term is equivalent to the negative expert cost, enabling the learning of a policy that can accurately reproduce the expert's behavior under constraints and obstacles. The proposed algorithm for EKMP converges to a stable local minimum, and its efficacy is demonstrated through simulations and real-world experiments on complex tasks involving multiple constraints and obstacles. Using machine learning image processing techniques, specifically a variation of the U-net algorithm, we enhance the sensitivity of all-sky maps from the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope by approximately 2.5 times over current methods. This improvement enables the detection of sources with fluxes 1.5 times lower than before. Notably, this method excels at identifying sources that change their brightness over time, such as the Crab Nebula, by accurately pinpointing them even when they are active and missing them when they are dormant. This technique also successfully eliminates fake sources and reduces noise, resulting in a more precise understanding of the sky. It can also identify sources that emit gamma-rays but are not visible in other wavelengths, such as the recently discovered Geminga-like pulsar PSR J1614-3230. This method can be applied to 11 years of data, revealing 1,000 to 2,000 variable sources, many of which were not identified before. This technique can be used to study sources that emit gamma-rays across the entire sky. A social welfare function can be optimized through various mechanisms, including auctions, voting systems, and algorithms, by achieving the maximum overall value when actions are taken sequentially. The most straightforward method to do this is a serial dictatorship, where each decision-maker's optimal choice is determined by their own self-interest, knowing their turn in the sequence of decisions. The challenge lies in designing a simple and efficient rule that determines the order in which decision-makers make their choices. We investigate the problem of optimizing a social welfare function by finding the most effective way to order the decision-makers, assuming that their preferences can be represented by any of the standard formats. We also consider the impact of side payments and the different possible orders in which decisions are made are considered. Theoretical results are applied to several real-world scenarios, including the allocation of frequencies in wireless communication networks, the assignment of tasks in workflow systems, and the solution to the multiple-killer-vehiel problem in surveillance. The findings can be used to develop efficient and fair voting systems, auctions, and algorithms for a wide range of applications. A well-designed tight-binding model has the potential to accurately capture light-matter interactions within semiconductors and dielectrics, enabling the simulation of photonic and phononic phenomena and interactions with matter. However, such models are only reliable if they remain gauge-invariant, as any loss of invariance can result in physically meaningless effects such as radiative decay of a ground state or the appearance of non-zero charge in a neutral system. Unfortunately, current tight-binding models often fail to meet this standard, leading to inaccuracies in their predictions. In this study, we present a comprehensive analysis of the sources of invariance failure in tight-binding models and propose a set of criteria for a model's gauge invariance. We then demonstrate the application of these criteria through a reconstruction of a tight-binding model for gallium arsenide, showing that the resulting model accurately captures the effects of light and maintains gauge invariance. This reconstituted model exhibits improved performance over existing TB models, particularly in terms of radiative decay rates. Furthermore, we investigate the influence of tight-binding model parameters on the photon dispersion relation and group velocity, highlighting the significance of gauge invariance in these calculations. This research provides a foundation for the development of accurate tight-binding models that can accurately capture light-matter interactions and related phenomena. Additionally, it underscores the importance of explicit gauge invariance in tight-binding models, which can be achieved through the parameterization of model parameters in terms of physical quantities such as electric and magnetic fields. This approach enables the simulation of photonic and phononic phenomena and interactions with matter, paving the way for the exploration of novel light-matter interactions and phenomena in semiconductors and dielectrics. This research is particularly relevant to the study of light-matter interactions in solids, which is an area of growing interest, with applications in optomechanics, opto-electronics, and quantum information processing. Furthermore, our test simulations demonstrate the significant potential of these formulas to streamline the restoration of symmetry within large and complex nuclear systems. Additionally, these derived expressions can be seamlessly integrated with the recently developed sphre code to efficiently perform self-consistent calculations that simultaneously account for both pairing and quadrupole correlations within heavy atomic mass regions. Notably, our results indicate that even in situations where several quasiparticle pairs are excited across multiple shells, the time required for a single-electron matrix element calculation remains remarkably short, amounting to roughly 0.01 seconds on a standard desktop computer. This marks a significant improvement over previous methods, which were often limited to pair-truncated Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov configurations due to their slower computation speeds. This advancement in computational efficiency now paves the way for more comprehensive studies of complex nuclear systems, including those involving quadrupole correlations within heavy atomic mass regions. This includes the ability to perform detailed analyses of shape phase transitions, as well as the coexistence of multiple quadrupole deformations, and even the study of exotic phenomena such as superdeformations and chirality. This achievement is particularly noteworthy because it provides a robust solution to the long-standing challenge of accurately computing matrix elements within multi-quasiparticle configurations, which has hindered the development of a self-consistent and unified framework for describing complex nuclear systems. This breakthrough has significant implications for our understanding of heavy atomic mass regions, which are characterized by intricate quadrupole shell structures and multiple coexisting quasiparticle configurations. Neural network-based point cloud models have achieved remarkable accuracy in various tasks such as classification, detection, and segmentation. However, these models are prone to overfitting due to limited training data and are sensitive to noise in real-world data. To address this challenge, we propose a novel technique called Transformation-PC (TPC) that incorporates a transformation-based smoothing framework specifically designed for point clouds. TPC utilizes a simple yet effective transformation layer to map points to a lower-dimensional space and then combines two noise-reducing operations: total variation regularization and the median filter, to enhance robustness against noise. By integrating TPC with point set neural networks through a transformation layer, we demonstrate significant improvements in classification accuracy and robustness against noise and outliers in K-NN and R-KNN datasets. Furthermore, our results indicate that TPC-based models achieve comparable or better performance compared to state-of-the-art point cloud models, including PatchGCN, DGCNN, and PointASNL, while being more efficient and easier to implement. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuan-yang/TPC.

Recent studies have demonstrated the potential of prompt-based techniques to adapt Transformers for task-conditioning without requiring task-specific parameters. Existing methods employ fixed prompts that are either manually crafted or generated through learning, but these approaches have limitations, particularly when dealing with multiple tasks simultaneously. In contrast, our proposed HyperPrompt framework learns task-conditioning prompts in a hierarchical manner, utilizing both global and local prompt generators to produce high-quality prompts that are both effective and efficient. By integrating a prompt generator selector, HyperPrompt can dynamically choose the optimal prompts for each input sample, leading to enhanced performance. We evaluate HyperPrompt on the GLUE benchmark, achieving superior results compared to state-of-the-art prompt-based methods and demonstrating its capability to generalize across datasets. Furthermore, HyperPrompt exhibits superior data efficiency, as evidenced by our experiments on the larger SuperGLUE dataset. We believe HyperPrompt represents a significant advancement in prompt-based task-conditioning and can serve as a foundation for exploring more complex prompt generation architectures. We also introduce HyperPrompt-Decoder, an extension of HyperPrompt that incorporates a decoder for generating prompts, leading to improved performance on certain tasks. This variant can be viewed as a decoder-only version of HyperPrompt, and we provide a detailed analysis of the differences between HyperPrompt and HyperPrompt-Decoder. We make the HyperPrompt code and models publicly available at https://github.com/THU-ICML-Hub/HyperPrompt.

Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms like lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. However, compared to tree-building methods, constructing phylogenetic networks is a more complex task, with few methods available to infer them directly from data. As a result, researchers often resort to converting reconstructed phylogenetic trees into networks using various methods, with little information available about the inherent topological characteristics of these converted networks. This is followed by a careful stage, where we refine the selected knowledge based on semantic relationships. Through extensive experiments on the CommonsenseQA dataset, our approach has shown significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our results indicate that simply incorporating the semantic knowledge can sometimes lead to incorrect answers, underscoring the importance of careful selection. This is further supported by an in-depth analysis of our model's performance. This work is a pioneering effort to explore the role of semantic knowledge in open-domain question answering, and our findings provide valuable insights for future research in this area. A comprehensive analysis of cometary spectra reveals that the majority of observed features can be attributed to neutral atoms and molecules as well as singly and doubly charged ions. Among these, the most prevalent are carbon-based species, hydrogen-based species, and oxygen-based molecular ions. Notably, the most abundant oxygen-based molecular ions in the solar system are often lacking in current cometary spectra databases, which are primarily constructed from laboratory measurements and observations of the interstellar medium. As a result, there is a significant knowledge gap in the spectral characteristics of these oxygen-based molecular ions, particularly in the ultraviolet and visible ranges. To address this, we have compiled a comprehensive list of the most abundant oxygen-based molecular ions in the solar system, along with their relevant spectral characteristics, which can be used to enhance the accuracy of cometary spectra models and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the chemical composition of comets. Furthermore, this database can be applied to the analysis of cometary spectra from space-based telescopes, such as the Hubble Space Telescope, which can offer valuable insights into the physical and chemical processes occurring within comets. This database is particularly useful for the upcoming Comet Interactor for Spectral and Temporal Analysis (CISTA) instrument on the James Webb Space Telescope, which will be capable of collecting high-resolution spectra of comets across a wide range of wavelengths. In contrast, we argue that such methods can result in poor performance due to the failure to account for source-side noise. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes a probabilistic source code to capture the variability in the source domain. Specifically, we propose a conditional distribution of target data given the source code, which enables us to generate accurate representations of the target data even in the presence of source-side noise. This approach is mathematically represented as a generative adversarial network (GAN) and is amenable to optimization through adversarial training. We evaluate our approach on multiple UDA benchmarks, including the Office-31 and Office-Home datasets, and demonstrate that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin. Notably, our approach achieves a 95.6% accuracy on the Office-31 dataset, which is a new state-of-the-art performance. Deep Neural Networks have achieved remarkable accuracy in various data analysis tasks, including but not limited to, image classification, sound recognition, and predicting particle interactions. However, assessing the reliability of their predictions proved more challenging and, until recently, lacked a standardized framework. In the context of traditional numerical methods, such as Finite Element Analysis, a similar uncertainty existed regarding the predictions of complex physical phenomena. Both scenarios share a common goal: to quantify the uncertainty in predictions and improve the accuracy of their models. This study aims to create a unified framework for evaluating the reliability of predictions made by Neural Networks and numerical solutions to physical problems, by introducing a common framework and set of evaluation metrics. Furthermore, we present a comprehensive comparison of various uncertainty quantification methods suitable for both Neural Networks and numerical solutions, including Monte Carlo methods, Deep Neural Networks, such as Deep Learning FEM, and more advanced techniques like Deep Data Driven Reduced Order Models. We demonstrate the performance of these methods on both a particle scattering problem and the classification of images using Neural Networks, and provide a comprehensive framework for evaluating and comparing these methods. This study is a significant contribution to the field of Uncertainty Quantification, and we believe it will be a valuable resource for both researchers and practitioners working in the field of Uncertainty Quantification in Scientific Machine Learning. By applying a Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation, the model is transformed into an Ising model in a $d$-dimensional cavity space. The cavity interaction decays with distance $r$ as $1/r^{2d-4}$ in both cases, and this decay rate determines the phase structure of the model. For $2d \leq 4$, the model exhibits a first-order phase transition, while for $d > 4$, it undergoes a continuous phase transition. The SU($N$) model displays a re-entrant phase transition at specific dimensions, and this phenomenon is absent in the U($N$) model. The phase diagrams of both models are compared, and we also investigate the effects of different symmetries on the phase structure. In contrast, the U($N$) unitary matrix model exhibits a first-order phase transition at $d = 3$, and this is also observed in the large $N$ limit. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are a key technology in image recognition, but their reliability is threatened by the increasing prevalence of hardware errors caused by aging infrastructure, electromagnetic interference, and other factors. This issue is exacerbated by the limited availability of accurate error rates for pre-trained CNNs. This research focuses on developing a hardware fault-tolerant system that uses activation range supervision to ensure the safety and efficiency of CNNs. By monitoring the output of each activation function, this approach detects and corrects errors without requiring precise error rates or retraining the network. This method has been successfully applied to a widely used pre-trained CNN, resulting in a 1.5x improvement in the number of error-free operations and a 1.2x increase in the number of errors corrected per activation function compared to existing solutions. This research demonstrates the feasibility of hardware fault-tolerant CNNs using activation range supervision and highlights the need for more efficient error detection mechanisms that can be integrated with existing deep learning frameworks. This research also provides a foundation for further investigation into the error behavior of CNNs and the development of more advanced fault-tolerant techniques. This paper presents a novel algorithm for a type of netting known as the "Guarantee Scheme Clearing Algorithm." The algorithm is specifically designed to address the financial obligations between Romanian companies and the Romanian state. The Guarantee Scheme, a program that provides financial protection to companies and their suppliers, has experienced significant growth, resulting in substantial financial obligations between participating parties. To efficiently manage these obligations, the algorithm is employed, ensuring that the total amount owed is minimized. This is achieved through a series of exchanges, or'swaps,' that allow parties with higher credit ratings to assume the debts of those with lower ratings, ultimately reducing the overall financial burden. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through a case study of the Romanian Guarantee Scheme, involving over 1,000 companies and $100 million in financial obligations. The results show a significant reduction in the total amount owed, with a potential savings of up to 50%. This highlights the algorithm's potential to be a valuable tool for managing complex financial obligations and facilitating cooperation among parties with varying credit ratings. The algorithm's design is modular and adaptable, making it suitable for application in various scenarios and industries. Current dialogue state tracking systems are vulnerable to performance degradation when trained on datasets containing labeling errors. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework called ASSIST that utilizes multiple sources of data to enhance robustness to noisy labels. By integrating a specialized module for detecting and downweighting unreliable labels, ASSIST significantly outperforms the baseline models across multiple evaluation metrics, including F1 score, overall accuracy, and the proportion of states that are accurately labeled. Notably, ASSIST achieves a notable 10% improvement in F1 score when trained on datasets with high label noise levels. Moreover, our framework demonstrates superior performance to state-of-the-art baselines, including models that employ self-supervised pre-training and specialized architectures for dialogue state tracking. The source code for ASSIST is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/THU-ICML/ASSIST. Additionally, we have made the dataset used in this study publicly accessible at https://github.com/THU-ICML/ASSIST-Dataset. This research contributes a novel dataset for dialogue state tracking, known as the MultiTask Dialogue State Tracking Dataset, which incorporates diverse dialogue scenarios and label noise levels. This dataset is designed to facilitate further research into dialogue state tracking in the presence of label noise. In this research, we introduce an advanced version of energy games, which is played on a finite and directed graph and features a special ordering among the players. The key distinction between this variant and traditional energy games lies in the presence of a total order that defines the players' relative positions and priorities. This ordering significantly affects the rules governing the players' available actions and objectives within the game's framework. Specifically, the order dictates that a player can only make a move if all higher-priority players have already taken their turn, and their actions are contingent upon the outcomes of those higher-priority players' moves. Moreover, the payoffs associated with each node are determined by the players' relative positions and the outcomes of the game. Our primary contribution is to demonstrate that determining the existence of a winning strategy for the first player in these energy games is equivalent to solving a specific type of linear program known as a totally unimodular integer program. Furthermore, we establish that this energy games variant retains the same level of computational tractability as standard energy games, which is characterized as being NP-complete but NP-complete in its own right. Additionally, we explore the scenario in which the players' positions are reversed and the impact of removing the total order on the game's solvability. Lastly, we provide a method for converting an energy game with a total order into an equivalent standard energy game through a transformation that maintains the game's solvability. This research provides a comprehensive examination of energy games under the constraint of a total order among the players. This variant of energy games offers an intriguing line of inquiry that has the potential to contribute to the broader study of energy games. We also examine several extensions of Jonsson's G\"{o}del modal logic, including the addition of propositional quantifiers, and provide their respective algebraic and relational semantics. Notably, we establish that the addition of propositional quantifiers to Jonsson's G\"{o}del modal logic results in a class of finite G\"{o}del algebras with modal operators that isomorphic to finite distributive lattices with propositional quantifiers. Furthermore, we provide a proof that the finite G\"{o}del algebras with modal operators and the finite G\"{o}del preimage algebras are isomorphism complete, and that they share the same first-order properties. We also discuss the relationship between Jonsson's G\"{o}del modal logic and its extensions and other modal logics, including Grigori's G\"{o}del modal logic, and the G\"{o}del modal logics with the B and W modalities. This study has led to the detection of two isomeric forms of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C$_5$H$_5$C$\equiv$N) in TMC-1, which was predicted by theoretical models. These values are comparable to those of CCH and CN derivatives of benzene and naphthalene found in the same source, indicating that the formation of these molecules is likely influenced by the ring size. This trend is consistent across cyclopentadiene, cycloheptadiene, benzene, and naphthalene molecules. We have also observed that the abundance of ethynyl cyclopentadiene is significantly lower than that of its protonated counterpart, which may be attributed to the steric hindrance caused by the presence of the ethynyl group. This study has expanded our knowledge of complex organic molecules in the TMC-1 star-forming region and has provided valuable insights into the chemistry of these molecules. In neural machine translation, the attention model is widely used to select relevant source sentences information to facilitate the target sentence generation. However, existing attention models typically focus on neighboring source sentence segments, which can lead to suboptimal performance. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel look-ahead attention model that enables the model to consider not only the current source sentence segment but also future segments. By incorporating this ability, the model can better capture long-distance source sentence dependencies and generate more accurate and fluent target sentences. Experimental results on two translation tasks demonstrate that our proposed look-ahead attention model outperforms the standard attention model and a strong baseline, including a state-of-the-art transformer model. Specifically, our model achieves a significant improvement of +1.35 in BLEU score on WMT'14 English-to-German translation and +0.67 on WMT'14 English-to-French translation. Code and models are available at https://github.com/zhengyangwang/lookahead-attention.

Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  However, when working with structured data, such as social networks and spatial grids, current Gaussian process methods fail to effectively leverage the inherent connectivity and geometric structure.  This limitation is addressed by introducing a new class of Gaussian processes that incorporate the principles of Mat\'ern kernels, commonly used in stochastic processes and Sobolev spaces, to the existing framework.  Through theoretical analysis and practical applications, we demonstrate that these new Gaussian processes offer improved performance and more interpretable results when working with structured data.  Specifically, we show that they are capable of modeling smoothness and anisotropy, and provide a method for automatically selecting hyperparameters.  This is further illustrated through a series of experiments, including a real-world study of disease spread, which highlights the benefits of these new Gaussian processes over traditional methods.  The code for these experiments is available online.  We also discuss potential applications and areas for future research in this area.
